verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cached publisher's PDF (degaris-1989-what-if-ai-succeeds). On p. 20 (PDF p. 4) it says: "In 20 years time, it will be commonplace to say that the twenty-first century will be dominated by the machine if humanity so chooses—and maybe even if not." That sentence predicts what people will commonly say. It is not a direct claim made in the author's voice. The record's statement turns it into "states that the 21st century may be dominated by the machine whether or not humanity chooses it", which drops that layer and widens "maybe even if not" into "whether or not".

On p. 21 (PDF p. 5), Scenario 2 opens: "The second scenario is probably more popular in science fiction. It is simply that the artilects will take over. Events might evolve too quickly for human beings to remain in control. If the artilects do take over..." The statement says the artilects take over "because events move too quickly for human control". That turns the text's "might" into a definite cause, and it leaves out that the article frames this scenario as the one popular in science fiction.

Both changes make the statement say more than the text, which the pack rules count as material. The pack's own W02 record for the same article does keep the "forecast of what others will say" distinction, so the W01 record is inconsistent with it.

The finding is therefore right. Its conclusion on the role also holds: the article sets out a scenario in which the artilects take over, which meets the criterion's "could replace or succeed", so articulates_proposition and earliest-located can stay.

In the source, that hedge ("I might not necessarily believe this scenario will prove realistic") is attached only to Scenario 1, his own Terras/Cosmists scenario. It is not attached to Scenario 2, the take-over scenario this record quotes.

The earliestNote in drafts/de-garis.json (line 2182) repeats the same paraphrase: "it states that the century may be dominated by the machine 'maybe even if not' chosen".

findings.problem: The contests stance is weak against W01 as worded ('will or could replace or succeed'). His last paragraph ranks it below another danger: 'The real danger ... is not machines ... usurping our role'. The quoted 'earmarks of an urban legend' sentence is defined in the text by that plausibility plus a shudder-inducing punch line, not by falsity. verdict.reasoning:
I checked the record against the cached Edge text (dennett-2015-singularity-urban-legend). Both quotes are verbatim and the locators are correct: "It has the earmarks of an urban legend" is in the first paragraph, and "The real danger, then, is not machines that are more intelligent than we are usurping our role as captains of our destinies." is in the last paragraph. The statement matches the text. The title calls it "an urban legend", it defines the Singularity as AI surpassing "its creators in intelligence and takes over the world", and the last paragraph says the real danger is "basically clueless machines being ceded authority".

On the stance, the finding does not hold for three reasons.

(1) The pack defines contests as "a text that disputes it or a premise it depends on" (propositions.json note). FORMAT.md also provides engagement.kind "contrary-only" for a contesting text that does not argue against a specific premise. The record uses that category openly. Its rationale and qualification therefore describe the kind of contest the pack's format allows. They do not concede that the stance is wrong.

(2) The text disputes the forecast, not only its priority. It calls the Singularity "a meme" with the earmarks of an urban legend and pairs it with a legend that is plainly false (sneeze, belch and fart at once and you die). It says it "has proven to be a remarkably persuasive escalation" of decades of hype that "you might think" would be "regarded as a parody, a joke". It treats the barricades and harbingers as "alarm calls". It sets the real problem at a "much closer tipping point". It describes current systems as "a mindless slave" and "clueless machines". The question-mark title is consistent with doubt about the forecast. That is a dispute of W01's credibility, stated without a premise argument, which is what contrary-only means.

(3) The proposed fix misuses the pack's categories. In propositions.json, bears_on is for "a text that comes close" to meeting the criterion. `missing` names "the element of the criterion the passage lacks" (FORMAT.md). Recording Dennett as bears_on would present him as coming close to articulating machine succession, which is the reverse of what the text says.

The phrase "Well, in principle I guess it's possible!" is the reaction a legend draws from its hearer, given as one of a legend's earmarks. It is not Dennett granting that the scenario is possible. So it cannot carry the finding's reading that he grants possibility and contests only importance.

A separate minor point, not the auditor's claim: the qualification's wording "Dennett grants the scenario 'a certain scientific plausibility'" slightly overstates his own concession for the same reason. It could read: "Dennett lists 'a certain scientific plausibility' among the earmarks of an urban legend and directs attention to a different risk; the record does not show that he holds succession impossible." This is wording polish and does not affect the stance.
verdict.fix: No stance change; keep contests_proposition with engagement "contrary-only". Optional minor wording change to the qualification: "Dennett lists \"a certain scientific plausibility\" among the earmarks of an urban legend and directs attention to a different risk; the record does not show that he holds succession impossible."

findings.problem: The statement turns a concessive clause into an assertion. It says biological intelligence 'is thrown from its perch' ('so that'), but the essay says 'even if thrown from its perch', inside a sentence denying the end of biological intelligence.
findings.evidence: 'However, to address often expressed concerns, this does not imply the end of biological intelligence, even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority.'
findings.proposedFix: Reword: '... states that most of the intelligence of our civilisation will ultimately be nonbiological and that this does not imply the end of biological intelligence "even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority", holding that the civilisation will remain human.'

verdict.reasoning:
I extracted the item from pack.json (source kurzweil-2001-loar, cached Kurzweil Library page) and read the passage in context: "Most of the intelligence of our civilization will ultimately be nonbiological, which by the end of this century will be trillions of trillions of times more powerful than human intelligence. However, to address often expressed concerns, this does not imply the end of biological intelligence, even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority. Moreover, it is important to note that the nonbiological forms will be derivative of biological design. In other words, our civilization will remain human..."

The essay's main claim in that sentence is a denial: the shift "does not imply the end of biological intelligence". "Even if thrown from its perch" sits inside that denial as a concessive clause. The record's statement drops the denial and turns the clause into a consequence the essay asserts ("so that biological intelligence is thrown from its perch"). It also uses the author's phrase in the pack's own voice without quotation marks. The statement therefore says more than the text, and it shifts the stance of the very sentence it relies on as evidence (evidence item 2). The qualification mentions the denial, but that does not fix a statement that misreports the passage.

The finding stands. By the pack rubric, "statement saying more than the text" counts as material, although the original auditor rated it minor. The locator and the two quoted passages are verbatim and correctly placed, so only the statement needs to change. The proposed rewording keeps the W01 articulation: most intelligence becomes nonbiological and biological intelligence loses its evolutionary primacy, now in quoted words attributed to Kurzweil. It also keeps the author's concessive framing.
verdict.fix: Replace the statement with: "Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that most of the intelligence of our civilisation will ultimately be nonbiological, and that this \"does not imply the end of biological intelligence, even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority\", holding that the civilisation will remain human." verdict.reasoning: I checked the item in pack.json against the cached source (lanier-2000-half-manifesto). The first evidence item quotes "That qualitative as well as quantitative aspects of information systems will be accelerated by Moore's Law." It is verbatim, and the locator (Heading "Belief #5") is correct. The essay introduces its numbered beliefs with "I will now examine the five beliefs that must precede acceptance of the new eschatology". Belief #1 carries the "Cybernetic Totalist" prefix, and the section under Belief #5 rejects the heading's claim: "If anything, there's a reverse Moore's Law observable in software". So the passage states the view Lanier disputes, not his own view. The item is marked support "supports" with note null. Nothing at item level says the wording is the opposing belief. The quoted passage also drops the "Belief #5:" label, so the only cue is the locator. Read alone, the evidence shows Lanier apparently asserting the proposition that the record says he contests. The record's qualification and engagement rationale explain the context, but evidence items are inspected one at a time. Where the pack quotes wording that is not the author's own position elsewhere, it adds an explanatory note (for example, Joy's item: "Joy's reading of Moravec, not Moravec's wording."). The passage is relevant because it names the belief being contested, so it does not have to be removed or reclassified. A note is the smallest correct fix. Severity is minor: the quote is accurate and the stance and date are right, but the item can mislead when read on its own.

I checked the record (pack.json records, W02), its source (cacheKey minsky-1994-robots-inherit) and the live mirror. All three quotes are verbatim at the stated locators. The page carries "(Scientific American, Oct, 1994 with some minor revisions)" and the footer "Last modified: Wed Jan 02 1997". The mirror's HTTP Last-Modified is Tue, 26 Jan 2016. The facts the finding relies on are correct, but none of them shows a defect in the record.

1) The policy says that where the wording survives only in a later copy, the record carries both dates, both dates are shown, and "the attested date decides which text is earliest located". The Minsky record does this: its date is 1994-10 and its attested date is 1997-01-02. The Moravec records do the same: 1979-02 with 2001-07-10, and 1989 with 2001-03-06. Their 2001 attested dates are later than 1997, so Minsky is earliest located under the rule as written. A reader who sees a 1994 headline above records dated 1979 and 1989 is seeing what the policy prescribes, since both dates are shown on every record.

2) Under "Scope once", qualifications say only what is particular to the record. They do not compare it with other records. "Order is not influence" also covers the sequence. The proposed addition would cross-reference other records, which the policy does not ask for, so leaving it out is not an error.

3) Taking the date from the page's own footer is disclosed. The source's version field names the web.mit.edu mirror, says the original address returns 404 and quotes the footer. The document's dateNote quotes the footer too, and the attested note says the date is when the web text was last modified. The broader question of whether the attested-date rule should apply to author-hosted copies is already an open question for the maintainer, in the moravec group. Saying the headline "depends on" that question is a remark about policy, not an error in this record.

The finding concedes that the headline is consistent with the policy, and the source bears out the record. It is not a real problem.

The cited passage (Ch. 1, printed p. 21, PDF p. 26) reads verbatim in the cached text (degaris-2005-artilect-war-wp): "...why I and other Cosmists feel so passionately about building artilects, that we are prepared to run the terrible risk of the extermination of the human species." The book uses "extermination" consistently for the risk the Cosmists accept: PDF p. 19 has "the extermination of the human species at the hands of the artilects", PDF p. 102 has "risk the start of an Artilect War and even the extermination of the human species", and PDF p. 213 has "a possible future extermination of the human species by artilects". "Extermination" names the artilects as the agents who would kill humans. "Extinction" drops that agent and softens the proposition. The author does write "human extinction at the hands of the artilects" once (PDF p. 225), but that is in a scenario comment, not in this record's evidence passage. So the statement does not say more than the text, but it swaps the author's own word in a sentence that otherwise follows the cited passage almost word for word. It also drops "terrible". This is a real but minor fidelity problem in the wording. It does not change the stance, attribution or date.

verdict.reasoning:
I extracted the record from pack.json and read the source myself (cacheKey degaris-essays-wp, PDF p. 87). The record contests W02, which per propositions.json covers texts holding that "the replacement or succession of human beings by machine intelligence" is undesirable or should be prevented. The record's statement is that Goertzel's gut reaction, faced with the choice between a godlike artilect at the cost of humanity and humanity's survival, is to choose humanity.

The source runs in this order: "But my gut reaction is: I'd choose humanity." Then comes the passage about his daughter: "I'm not going to will her death to create a superhuman artilect." Then: "Gut feeling: I'd probably sacrifice myself to create a superhuman artilect, but not my kids…. I do have huge ambitions and interests going way beyond the human race – but I'm still a human." So the second evidence passage directly expands on "I'd choose humanity". Its main point, "but not my kids", is a refusal to accept the deaths of later human generations to bring about an artilect. That refusal is the substance of the contest.

The first half is willingness to give up his own life. That is a personal sacrifice. It does not accept that machines should replace humanity, which is what W02 is about. So the passage does not cut against the contest in the way the finding says. Even read as mixed, the passage still bears on and backs the record's statement. The record's qualification already notes the self-sacrifice caveat ("Goertzel adds that he would probably sacrifice himself, not his children"), so the reader gets the nuance. Under the FORMAT.md schema, "support" is either supports or context, and "supports" fits a passage that backs the record's statement. Context is for passages that only frame it. The quote is verbatim and short, and the locator is correct. This is at most a matter of editorial preference, not an error.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the item against the cached PDF (bostrom-2004-future-human-evolution, p. 5). The finding holds. Right after the record's third quoted passage ("...complete absence of any type of being whose welfare has moral significance."), the text says: "What would make such a world valueless is not the fact that machines would have replaced biological humans. Whether a mind is implemented on biological neurons or on silicon processors seems to make no fundamental moral difference. Rather, the catastrophe would be that such a world would not contain even the right kind of machines, i.e. ones that are conscious and whose welfare matters." The second quoted passage, the "alien types of complexes" question, is followed at once by "The answer may depend on the precise nature of those alien complexes."

W02's criterion is that succession of humans by machine intelligence would be acceptable, "for example because ... the growth of intelligence matters more than its human form". Bostrom accepts half of that: he says substrate makes no fundamental moral difference. What he disputes is that the growth of intelligence or complexity is enough when conscious, morally significant beings are absent. The engagement rationale (it disputes the "Panglossian" premise that more intelligent or complex forms are valuable in themselves) is roughly right. But the record as a whole tags the paper as contesting W02, and neither the statement nor the qualification says that the paper does not object to replacement by machines as such. That leaves out a sentence that bears directly on the proposition, so the record says more than the text: a reader would take it as general opposition to machine succession. Under the pack's rules this counts as material.

The finding is also right that the statement's "minds smarter and more intricate" changes the text's "complex structures, some of which are much smarter and more intricate". The text uses these complexes as its example of beings that may lack conscious experience, so calling them "minds" goes beyond what it says. The other parts of the record are fine: the dating qualification, the scenario qualification and the neutral verbs. The quoted passages are verbatim.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cached Forbes text (forbes-2009-degaris) in the paragraph that begins "Imagine a world". It sits under the heading 'The Terrans will "First Strike"'. The passage reads: "A young mother who has just given birth may choose to add a grain of artilectual sand to her newly born baby's brain, converting it into an artilect. There is so much computing capacity in that grain of sand that she has effectively "killed" her baby. It is no longer human, but an artilect in human disguise." It goes on: "Imagine older parents watching their adult children becoming cyborgs ... The parents will feel they have lost them. The rise of the artilects and the cyborgs will be profoundly disruptive to human culture, creating deep alienation and hatred." The next paragraph argues that the Terrans will have to strike first.

1. Stance. W03 requires that a human mind could be transferred to, copied into or continued in a machine substrate, so that humans could become machine intelligences. This passage describes adding machine capacity to a newborn's brain. That is augmentation, not transfer or copying. It also says outright that the child is converted "into an artilect", which affirms the clause "human beings could themselves become machine intelligences" rather than disputing it. The text's point is that the result is "no longer human". It does not say whether the mind or person continues in the machine substrate, and the scare quotes around "killed" show that the author is not asserting a literal end of the person. So the record's engagement rationale ("Disputes the premise that the human person continues...") reads more into the passage than the text states.

The pack also treats similar passages differently. Warwick's "part-artilects" augmentation passage is recorded as bears_on, with missing set to say that augmentation is not transfer. De Garis's own 1989 brain-modification passage is recorded as articulating W03. Neither treatment supports calling this augmentation passage a contest.

2. Fidelity. The statement says the mother "has effectively killed it". The text has effectively "killed", in scare quotes. Dropping the quotation marks makes the statement more literal than the text, so it says more than the source.

3. Context. The passage serves the section's argument about the forecast Terran alienation and first strike, and it ends with how parents "will feel". The qualification does not say this.

The finding holds. The first two problems are material.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked both parts against the cached PDF (chalmers-2010-singularity) and the pack's records. Both hold.

1. The statement says more than the text. On PDF p. 51 the quoted words are the consequent of a conditional: "Overall: I think that if a further-fact view is correct, then the status of destructive and reconstructive uploading is unclear, but there is good reason to take the optimistic view of gradual uploading." The p. 53 "Upshot" opens: "Speaking for myself, I am not sure whether a further-fact view or a deflationary view is correct." It then gives each branch separately: if the further-fact view is correct, "gradual uploading plausibly suffices for survival"; if the deflationary view is correct, "gradual uploading is close to as good as ordinary survival". On the deflationary view as Chalmers sets it out on pp. 51-52, there is no "Edenic" survival. That view also "combines elements of the optimistic and pessimistic view". So the record's unconditional "concludes that there is good reason to take the optimistic view that a person survives gradual uploading" turns a conditional, explicitly undecided conclusion into a flat one. The qualification mentions only destructive and reconstructive uploading and does not cure this. A statement saying more than the text could be argued to be material. The other auditor's "minor" is defensible because the stance is still articulation, but the fix is needed either way.

2. The attested date is inconsistent. The record's attested.date is 2010-06-13, taken from a capture that its own note says "was not compared". Elsewhere the pack uses the retrieval date when a capture could not be compared, and names the capture in the note. This applies to ht-w01/w02/w10-moravec-1991-universal-robot, ht-w01/w02-moravec-2000-robots-re-evolving-mind, ht-w02-bostrom-2004-future-of-human-evolution-contests and others, all with 2026-10-31. Editorial policy also says an archive link alone does not authenticate earlier bytes. The same defect is in ht-w02-chalmers-singularity. I accept the other auditor's word that the earliest-located holder does not change, so this part is minor.

findings.problem: The foreword does not dispute the proposition, which says the division could lead to war. Warwick hopes de Garis is wrong and offers a cyborg alternative. In the same foreword he says the reasoning is persuasive and that readers may doubt his own optimistic scenario. A hope is not a denial that war could follow. The engagement rationale ('Disputes the premise that the choice divides humans into two camps') says more than the text, and the qualification leaves out his statements in the other direction.

Hugo's reasoning is frighteningly persuasive, even though my viscera reject what he is saying.'; 'I hope that he will be shown to have been wrong'.

Or keep contests with engagement contrary-only, and in the qualification state that Warwick calls the reasoning 'frighteningly persuasive' and doubts that his own scenario will prevail.

verdict.reasoning:
I read the full foreword (cache degaris-2005-artilect-war-wp, PDF pp. 3–5). The criterion of W04 is modal: the disagreement "will divide human beings into opposed political groups, and could lead to large-scale war". The ontology defines contests_proposition as a passage that "disputes the proposition or a premise it depends on". Warwick's foreword does not do that.

1. He does not deny that war could follow. He writes "I sincerely hope it will not come to this sort of end game", "I firmly hope he is wrong, dead wrong" and "I hope that he will be shown to have been wrong". These are hopes, not denials. A hope that war will not happen does not dispute "could lead to".

2. In the same foreword he leans the other way. He writes "serious doubts may well arise as to whether my more optimistic scenario is more likely to win out. Hugo's reasoning is frighteningly persuasive, even though my viscera reject what he is saying", and he states the conditional "if Hugo's vision is correct". He also opens by saying he shares de Garis's belief that humanity "will have to confront the prospect of being replaced by a new dominant species".

3. The engagement rationale says more than the text. Warwick does not dispute that the choice divides humans into two camps. He places himself in the division ("I said that Terran was nearer the mark"), refers to the "Cosmist-Terran opinion spectrum", and calls himself a "Cyborgian". The cyborg path is introduced as a hope ("I hope that by enhancing ourselves … without having to pay the cost of a major war") and as "a sort of compromise". He gives no reason why the division would not form.

4. The qualification ("Stated as hope and alternative scenario in a foreword that also recommends the book") is true but incomplete. It leaves out his statements that the reasoning is persuasive and that his own scenario may not prevail, so the record reads as a firmer contest than the text supports.

The quotations themselves are verbatim, and the statement sentence is accurate as far as it goes. The fault is the predicate, the role and the engagement: wrong stance, and a rationale that says more than the text. The finding stands as material.

- predicate: bears_on_proposition
- roles: ["context"]
- engagement: null
- missing: "No statement that the division or a war will not or could not occur; Warwick states a hope that de Garis's forecast is wrong and a hoped-for alternative of human self-enhancement."
- statement: "Warwick's foreword to de Garis's The Artilect War (2005) states his hope that de Garis's forecast of a major war is wrong and that humans can reach artilect abilities by enhancing themselves without such a war; it also states that de Garis's reasoning is 'frighteningly persuasive'."
- qualification: "Stated as a hope and an alternative scenario. The same foreword states that readers may doubt 'whether my more optimistic scenario is more likely to win out', calls de Garis's reasoning 'frighteningly persuasive', and recommends the book."
- evidence: keep the two existing quotations. Optionally add (Foreword, p. ii, PDF p. 4): "serious doubts may well arise as to whether my more optimistic scenario is more likely to win out. Hugo's reasoning is frighteningly persuasive, even though my viscera reject what he is saying."

verdict.reasoning:

1) The role is per proposition, not per term. docs/ontology.md (line 169) says: "when any record's evidence uses a usual name, exactly one earliest-located-term record whose evidence contains that name and before which no such use is dated". It also says "Earliest located is decided by the date of the wording: the attested date where one is recorded". The validator in src/domain/schema.ts (around line 2353) does the same. It allows one term record per proposition. It matches every one of the proposition's terms against the evidence passages. 2) The After Life record's own wording is attested only from 2026-10-31. Its attested.note says so, and the pack.json source entry says the 1999-11-10 capture was not compared.

In ht-w03-mcginn-1999-hello-hal, dated 1999-01-03 with no attested date, the second evidence passage reads "...unknowingly extinguishing our consciousness by uploading into machines that are inherently incapable of feeling anything." So the record does not meet the ontology's condition that the term record's evidence contain the name.

findings.problem: The two quotations total 18 words from a 162-word source, about 11%, just over the 'about 10%' limit for documents under 2,000 words. The 162 words include the quoted message from Moss and the signature, so the share of Yudkowsky's own text is higher still.

verdict.reasoning:

- "Their futuristic projections/remedies are so utterly unrealistic" is 7 words when split on whitespace (src/domain/schema.ts wordCount).
- "Cosmists versus Terrans? What planet did these guys grow up on?" is 11 words.
- Together that is 18 unique quoted words.

The recorded documentWords of 162 checks out. It counts everything from "Bryan Moss wrote:" through the signature, including Moss's quoted notice and the ">" markers. Yudkowsky's own paragraph is 111 words, so 162 already overstates the base.

The admission validator settles it. In src/domain/schema.ts, maxQuotedWords(162) = floor(162/10) = 16. The only exception in withinQuotationLimit is a single complete sentence of up to 25 words that is the only passage quoted, and this record has two passages, so it does not apply. 18 is over 16, so these quotes would fail schema validation at admission. This is not just a judgment call about "about 10%".

The pack's own checker hid the problem. research/heterodox-thought/tools.mjs (line ~319) computes the limit for a document under 2,000 words as Math.max(25, floor(doc*0.1)). For this source that gives 25, so 18 words passed. The policy and schema.ts allow 25 words only as one sentence quoted on its own, so the checker is too loose. It can pass other short-source overruns in this pack as well.

Severity: minor, as reported, because the substance and attribution are correct. But the record must be fixed before admission. The statement itself is fine: "utterly unrealistic" is unquoted paraphrase, and "Cosmists versus Terrans" is the author's quoted wording.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the record against the cached text (gw-no-theory-of-ai) and the ontology definition of contests_proposition ("a passage disputes the proposition or a premise it depends on").

1. The finding misreads the sentence it relies on. "His argument may not be wrong, but it should be recognized for what it is…" comes at the end of the paragraph about Land's response to the orthogonality thesis ("terminal goals don't matter because AI will converge to a will-to-think"). "His argument" is that will-to-think argument, not the identification of capitalism with machine intelligence. So the post does not decline to dispute W06. The sentence belongs to a different proposition.

2. The post does dispute the W06 identification, and it gives reasons. The TL;DR says calling AI "capitalism" is "neither a sufficient nor useful descriptor". The body objects that in Land's view "there is only one artificial intelligence … and that is market capitalism", and that "All variation over agents, harnesses, implementations, it all dissolves into the totality of capital". It calls this "the Landian circle". It closes with "we know what capitalism does and where it can head. We have much more uncertainty about where AI leads", which treats AI and capitalism as distinct. That is a reason given against the identity premise. Land's own W06 articulation in the pack is "the teleological identity of capitalism and artificial intelligence" (ht-w06-land-2014-teleological-identity), and the post argues directly against that identity.

3. The record does not overstate. Its statement is two verbatim quotes, attributed and dated. The engagement rationale is narrow and accurate: it disputes that identifying AI with capitalism describes AI adequately, because the identification leaves no room for a plurality of intelligences. engages-premise fits the ontology's definition, since the message gives a reason against a premise. The qualification already notes that replies dispute the post's reading of Land and that the author later wrote he engaged too little with Land's posts.

The only arguable gap is narrow. The post denies that capital is the only or a sufficient account of AI, and it never says outright that capitalism is not an intelligence. But the rationale states exactly that scope, so this is not a material stance error. Downgrading the record to bears_on with a "may not be wrong" qualification would misattribute that sentence.
verdict.fix: No change needed. Do not add "His argument may not be wrong" to this record: in the post it refers to Land's will-to-think response to the orthogonality thesis, not to the identification of capitalism with AI.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked this against the cached texts and pack.json, and the finding holds as a minor date-basis problem.

**What the pages show**
- `moravec-1993-age-of-robots` (Robot93.html) is headed "June 1993 by Hans Moravec".
- `moravec-1998-simconex` is headed "Simulation, Consciousness, Existence -- Hans Moravec, 1998".
- Neither page says when it was put online.

**What the pack records**
- Both records have `time.basis: "posting"`.
- Both documents have `dateBasis: "posting"`.
- The notes say only "Date at the head of the author's page" and "Year at the head of the author's page".
- In FORMAT.md, `date` is "the date the work is dated by". The basis values are publication, posting, signature, delivery and submission. "Posting" says when something was posted on the web. The posting-basis entries for non-Moravec documents in the pack generally rest on a stated posting or post date ("Posted June 6, 2023", Substack post dates, `article:published_time`), not on an author's heading date.
- Recording "posting" here therefore asserts something the page does not show. For a 1993 heading it is also implausible, given the 1994 Extro 1 printing. For the 1998 page, the year more likely dates this version (the author's list gives a 1996 Telepolis original) than the upload.
- The same draft (moravec.json) treats equivalent author-printed dates on Moravec's own pages as "publication":
  - Pigs in Cyberspace: "The page gives '1992'"
  - After Life: "© 1989", an informal report
  - The Universal Robot: "© July 1991"
- So the posting basis on these two records is unsupported and inconsistent with the rest of the draft.

**Impact**
- The dates themselves (1993-06, 1998) are correctly transcribed.
- The quotes are verbatim and the earliest-located dating is not affected.
- Severity is minor (date basis), not material.

**Same issue on two other documents in the draft (not part of the finding)**
- `moravec-2000-robots-re-evolving-mind`: "The page is headed 'December 2000'"
- `moravec-1999-singularity-equations`: "The page is headed 'Hans Moravec, February 1999'"
- Both are recorded as posting on the same heading-date evidence.

Paragraph 8 contains "Capitalism, in contrast, has no external limit, it has consumed life and biological intelligence to create a new life and a new plane of intelligence, vast beyond human anticipation."

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cached publisher's PDF (degaris-1989-what-if-ai-succeeds) against W09's criterion: "the rise of machine intelligence is an expression of a physical, evolutionary or cosmological process larger than humanity".

Both evidence items are quoted verbatim and located correctly, but neither meets the criterion in the author's voice.

1. p. 17. After "For the first time, we are able to pose the question, What is humanity for?", the author calls it "a real one concerned with the choice about whether humanity will or will not serve as the stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution." This poses an open question about a human choice. The evolutionary step is only a presupposition of the question. The text does not state that the rise of the artilect expresses a process larger than humanity. Treating it as a "choice" points the other way.

2. p. 20 ('Options'). "However, a lot of people will start seeing humanity as a stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution and will claim it is humanity's destiny..." This forecasts what other people will think. The second half of the same sentence is the evidence for ht-w02-degaris-1989, which the pack correctly classes as bears_on, with missing: "The passage forecasts that others will hold the view; it does not itself state…". Counting the same forecast as the author's articulation for W09 is inconsistent with that treatment.

The rest of the article has no author-voice passage that rescues the record. "the next stage in the great upward movement toward . . . toward what?" is what the Cosmists "will feel". The p. 4 Darwinian passage says artilects "might choose" Darwinian self-modification, which is not a cosmic or larger-than-human process.

The pack concedes the weakness itself. The record's qualification calls the framing "the question the article poses" and "a view the author forecasts others will hold". The de Garis searchLog entry for W09 says "later texts (2001, 2005) state the evolutionary framing in the author's own voice", which implies the 1989 text does not.

The policy says a stance is what the text states, and inferences from presupposition are an escalation trigger. Since this record carries the W09 earliest-located headline, the defect is material. The finding holds.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked both passages against the cached text (williams-srnicek-2013-accelerate). Both are verbatim and at the stated places. Section 03, item 7 reads: "our position is that technology should be accelerated precisely because it is needed in order to win social conflicts." Section 02, paragraph 2 reads: "However Landian neoliberalism confuses speed with acceleration."

The finding misreads how the pack is built.

1. **The record type allows a missing element.** The record is `bears_on_proposition` with role `context` and a `missing` field. FORMAT.md defines `missing` as "bears_on only: the element of the criterion the passage lacks". So a bears_on record is meant for a passage that lacks an element of the criterion, and saying so in `missing` is that mechanism working, not an admission that the record is out of scope. W08 uses the same pattern several times: Moravec 1979, Land "Meltdown", the Lê/Land conversation of 2026 and bayes 2026 are all bears_on/context records whose `missing` says the passage does not mention machine intelligence or does not call for acceleration.

2. **The scope names this text.** scope.md lists "Srnicek and Williams's manifesto (2013)" by name in the accelerationism search bounds.

3. **The criterion is wider than machine intelligence.** W08 covers acceleration of "the technological and economic process that produces" machine intelligence. A passage holding that technology in general should be accelerated bears on that, even though it does not complete the criterion. The `missing` field states that gap correctly.

The wording complaints do not hold either:

- "as a means of winning social conflicts" closely paraphrases the manifesto's own words ("needed in order to win social conflicts") and is attributed to the manifesto. It reports what the text says. It does not describe a political position in the pack's own words.
- "distinguishes this from capitalist speed" is supported by the Section 02 passage, where the manifesto says Land's view "confuses speed with acceleration".
- "Landian neoliberalism" is a verbatim quotation attributed to the manifesto. The rules ban labels in the pack's own wording, not quoted words of the text's authors.
- Nothing here is Land's later political writing; the text is Williams and Srnicek's.

A stylistic preference for a different second quotation is not a rule violation.
verdict.fix: No change needed. Optional polish only: the qualification's phrase "the manifesto's political programme" could read "the manifesto's programme" to keep the pack's own descriptive words to a minimum. The rules do not require this.
